author: mark-n-hoffman
description: In 1990, the UN cut Iraq off from world trade to make Saddam Hussein back down without firing a shot. Ten years later, raw sewage was pouring into the rivers and hospitals were losing their doctors.

hero.hook: An embargo does not fire a single shot. In Iraq, it still made the water dangerous to drink.

blocks.text: To make a government back down without sending in the army, there is a weapon: [[economic sanctions]]. Ban its oil sales, freeze its assets, block its purchases of machinery, including what it needs to treat water. In **2015**, Barack Obama argued that this pressure had brought Iran to the table: Tehran limited its nuclear program in return for sanctions relief.

How does the pressure work? A targeted government may give in to regain access to its funds. But the effects quickly spill beyond the leaders: ordinary people can no longer afford food or find medicine, and water systems break down for lack of parts. Iraq in the **1990s** lived through exactly that.

The UN Charter keeps the two registers apart. Article 41 authorizes measures "not involving the use of armed force," such as cutting economic relations; Article 42 allows military action if those measures prove inadequate. Hence the habit of presenting sanctions as an alternative to war.

Sanctions work through rules imposed on banks and businesses: no payments to the targeted government, no sales of machinery to it either. When the [[UN Security Council]] adopts them, every member state has to enforce them. The promise of lifting them is the bait.

blocks.caption: Kuwaiti oil wells burning in 1991: the war drove Iraq out of Kuwait, the embargo stayed.

blocks.text: In August **1990**, after Iraq invaded Kuwait, the Council banned almost all trade with Baghdad. Cut off from its oil sales, the regime of [[Saddam Hussein]] lost its revenue: its opponents hoped to force it to withdraw. Iraqi troops were driven out in the **1991** [[Gulf War]], but the embargo remained, now conditional on the elimination of weapons of mass destruction. Yet Iraq lived on its oil, which paid for its imported food: less revenue meant less food and fewer public services.

The war had damaged the power stations and water systems. Repairing them required imported equipment, but the UN sanctions committee held up some of those purchases. In **2000**, the UN secretary-general himself urged the committee to release the water and sanitation equipment.

blocks.caption: A water treatment plant in Ramadi, Iraq, seen from the air: facilities like this depend on imported parts.

blocks.text: That same year, the UN estimated that nearly **90%** of the raw sewage from Iraq's pumping stations was flowing straight into the rivers, exposing everyone who depended on them to disease. Repairs were already difficult, with little money and few trained staff. On top of that, sanctions delayed the equipment needed: they acted as another mechanism of violent coercion, not as its alternative.

sections.title: When clean water is at stake

blocks.text: As the economy collapsed, families struggled to feed themselves. Oil revenue had also paid public salaries: poorly paid doctors and teachers changed jobs or left the country, and hospitals and schools ran short of staff. According to the UN, most Iraqis were struggling to survive, while a few people close to power kept their standard of living.

blocks.caption: Iraqi women line up for food handed out by U.S. and Iraqi soldiers, in the 2000s.

blocks.text: In **1995**, the [[Oil-for-Food Programme]] allowed Iraq to sell oil, under UN supervision, to buy food, medicine and civilian supplies. Shortages eased, but a humanitarian program is no substitute for a working economy. A UN panel even found that dependence on rations had tightened the government's grip: Iraqis came out poorer and more dependent on the very regime being targeted.

Many families who survived the bombing of 1991 later fell seriously ill from drinking contaminated water, for lack of the equipment that sanctions had delayed. Those sanctions inflicted physical harm on civilians, even as they were defended as a nonviolent alternative to war. Since **2004**, the UN has in fact preferred targeted sanctions, asset freezes and travel bans, which spare the population.

events.title: Targeted sanctions

blocks.text: The choice between "sanctions or war" itself does violence to our ability to think. If those are the only two thinkable options, evidence that both harm civilians is used to pick the lesser evil, not to rethink the options. This is [[structural violence]]: it sets the terms of the debate in advance and rules out some responses before they are even examined. Policies that starve people or make them sick then look necessary.
Presented as a peaceful alternative to war, the sanctions on Iraq made the water dangerous and emptied the hospitals: another form of violence, and one civilians suffered first.
